sections.h2: Which office holds the land records?
sections.html:
The clerk of the county containing the house holds them. In Texas the county clerk doubles as the recorder, and also serves as secretary to the commissioners court and filer of probate matters.

A seller living in Dallas with a house in another county therefore deals with the second county's clerk. Texas has 254 counties, and each runs its own index. Some post searchable images online and others expect a visit, so call the clerk's office before planning a trip.

sections.h2: What kinds of papers end up in the deed records?
sections.html:
Ownership transfers and the paper that surrounds them. Recorded deed types include general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds. Affidavits, loan releases, leases, sales contracts and powers of attorney sit alongside them.

  • Deeds that pass ownership from one party to another.
  • Deeds of trust that secure a loan, and the releases that end them.
  • Notices of a lender's auction, filed by the clerk ahead of the sale.
  • State tax lien notices from the Comptroller, which the clerk enters in a state tax lien book.
  • Court papers that carry title after a death.

A title search reads all of these in order, which is why a house with a messy record can take longer to close.

sections.h2: What a deed must show to be filed
sections.html:
A signature plus an acknowledgment, or a sworn statement before two witnesses who sign too. Property Code section 12.001(b) governs, and notaries, clerks and county court judges are among those who can take an acknowledgment.

A deed missing that step may be refused. Leaving out the buyer's mailing address can add a fee. Compare names on the new deed with the name on the last recorded deed, because small differences, such as a dropped middle initial, lead to questions at closing. Title companies and attorneys normally draft the deed so such points get checked first.

sections.h2: Recording fees at the clerk's counter
sections.html:
The base amounts are set by statute, with county add-ons on top. These are the 2023 figures.

Typical Texas county recording charges, 2023 schedule
Recording chargeAmount
First page of an instrument$5.00
Each added page, part of a page or attachment$4.00
Each name beyond five that must be indexed$0.25
Records management and preservationNo more than $10
Records archiveNo more than $10
Records technology and infrastructure$2.00
Filing a foreclosure sale notice$2.00 per notice

A commissioners court may direct the clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain federal or state grant programs. Call the clerk or check its website for the current schedule.

sections.h2: Transfer tax and property tax at closing
sections.html:
Recording charges are the only deed filing costs the clerk lists. Confirm the full cost list for your closing with the clerk or a title company.

Property tax is its own cost. Each year's tax lien arises at the new year, and the person who owned the house then remains liable even after a sale. A closing therefore divides the year's tax between the parties, and a title search checks earlier years for unpaid amounts.

sections.h2: How liens and sale deeds show up
sections.html:
A mortgage shows up as a recorded deed of trust, and paying it off should produce a recorded release. If the lender never filed the release, the old deed of trust still turns up in a search and may need clearing before you can sell.

Tax matters leave other marks. The yearly property tax lien arises without any filing, while a state tax lien is a recorded notice. Deeds from tax sales are filed with the clerk too, and the filing date starts the redemption clock. Homestead, agricultural and mineral property can be redeemed for two years from the filing of the purchaser's deed, with a 25 percent premium in the first year and 50 percent in the second, plus other costs. Other property follows a shorter 180-day window.

  • Deeds of trust and releases.
  • State tax lien notices.
  • Tax foreclosure deeds and sheriff's deeds.
  • Any judgment or contractor claim that the clerk has indexed.

sections.h2: Records after a death or a foreclosure
sections.html:
What lands in the records after a death depends on the route the family took. Administration leaves an executor's or administrator's deed, a muniment leaves the court order and will, and a transfer on death deed leaves an affidavit of death with the death certificate. The clerk cannot add heirs to an earlier deed.

Foreclosure leaves a separate trail. The lender posts a notice at the courthouse and files a copy with the clerk at least three weeks before the sale. The commissioners court designates the sale area and records it. Sales are held between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., normally on the month's first Tuesday, and the buyer's trustee deed is recorded afterward like any other deed.

sections.h2: What a former owner can reclaim after a sale
sections.html:
Sometimes money is left over. Following a tax foreclosure sale, the former owner has two years to claim any surplus. Following a lender's sale, junior lienholders are paid first and the former owner gets what remains.

A borrower can face a deficiency suit, which must be filed within two years of the sale, and may ask for a fair market value offset. Redemption after a lender's sale exists only for certain kinds, such as owners' association assessment liens. Recorded deeds show the sale date, so the dates in the clerk's records are the starting point for every one of these deadlines.

Someone still living in a house after a sale may face an eviction case, which is a court matter and not a records question. The buyer's deed in the land records is the proof the buyer would show.

Bring the owner's full name as it appears on the last deed, the property address and, if you have it, the recording date or instrument number. Clerks can search by name or by instrument number, and a title company can order the same copies for you.

Ask for copies of the vesting deed, every open deed of trust and any release. Plain copies are fine for your own review, but a title company may want certified ones. Expect a per-page copy charge, and ask whether the office takes cards or checks only.

sections.h2: Reviewing the record before you list
sections.html:
Pull the latest deed and any open deed of trust, then ask a title company or the clerk for a search. Finding a defect early leaves time to fix it.

  • Match the owner's name on the deed to the name used on the listing.
  • Locate the deed of trust and confirm the payoff or release.
  • Ask whether any state tax lien notice is on file.
  • Look up the appraisal district record for owner of record and exemptions.
  • For an inherited house, confirm the probate paper is recorded in the right county.

These steps cost little and often save weeks at the closing table for a Texas seller.

faqs.a: The clerk for the land's county, who acts as recorder for deeds, loan documents, liens and sale notices.

faqs.q: What does filing a deed cost at the clerk's counter?
faqs.a: The 2023 schedule shows $5.00 for the opening page and $4.00 for each page after it, plus capped add-ons. The clerk's current schedule gives the total.

faqs.q: What must a Texas deed carry to be recorded?
faqs.a: A signature with an acknowledgment, or a sworn statement before two witnesses. A notary can take the acknowledgment, as can some other officers.

faqs.q: Can a clerk write heirs onto an old deed?
faqs.a: No. A new instrument, such as an executor's deed, muniment order or affidavit of death, has to be recorded.
The notice must be on the courthouse door and with the clerk 21 days or more before the sale. Filing it with the clerk carries a $2.00 fee.
